listing_view.reasoning: Subscription built to ~70x by close (from near zero on day one), which points to strong demand and a likely pop, though I have no grey market premium or anchor data to confirm pricing quality. The offer is priced at ~36x latest EPS versus a peer median of ~103x, so the seller has left headline room on the table relative to the comparison it chose. My score is capped by the absence of anchor/GMP evidence and by the fact that a hot subscription book says nothing about whether the price was fair.

longterm_view.reasoning: Reported growth and returns are spectacular on paper (PAT CAGR ~170%, ROCE ~70%), but profit is not converting to cash: latest-year operating cash flow was ₹258m against ₹1,804m EBITDA, an EBITDA-to-cash conversion of ~0.14, and one of the three years had negative operating cash flow. Top-10 customers are ~93% of revenue [business, page 246], so the growth rests on a very narrow buyer base. This pattern — surging accounting profit, weak cash, high customer concentration — is exactly the profile that needs scepticism even when the sector story is real.

governance.reasoning: The extracts show standard boilerplate: promoters attest no conflict of interest with suppliers and that related-party dealings are disclosed in Note 40 [promoters, page 311][promoters, page 312], and there are criminal-proceedings sections concerning promoters with no detail visible in the extracts [litigation, page 420]. The company itself flags ongoing related-party transactions as a risk [related_party, page 414]. I cannot score this high on attestations alone, nor low without the underlying disclosures, which I was not given.

key_risks.risk: Profits are not turning into cash
key_risks.why_it_matters: Latest operating cash flow is ~14% of EBITDA and ~20% of PAT, and one recent year was negative, so either working capital is absorbing everything or the reported earnings quality is weaker than the P&L suggests.
Top 10 customers supplied 93-95% of revenue across all three years, so losing or renegotiating with one or two buyers could reverse the growth story quickly.

Receivable days of ~118-158 mean a large, growing chunk of the sales surge is owed money, which is the mechanical explanation for the poor cash conversion and a classic place for earnings inflation to hide.
The company itself flags heightened competition for critical raw materials, which threatens the recently expanded 27.6% EBITDA margin that the valuation implicitly extrapolates.
The prospectus expects related-party dealings to continue, and with a promoter-heavy mainboard IPO that is where margin and cash can quietly leak.

answers.question: is the peer set fairly chosen, and are the peers themselves expensive rather than this being cheap?
answers.answer: The peer set skews expensive: the six chosen comparators carry P/Es of 32 to 160 with a median of ~103, and several (Hitachi Energy at ~160x, Schneider Infra at ~155x, CG Power at ~115x) are hotly-valued large caps, while the obvious closest comparable by size and business, Transformers & Rectifiers, trades at ~32x — near this IPO's own ~36x. So 'cheap at 0.35x the peer median' is largely an artefact of a peer set priced for a sector mania; against the most comparable peer the discount disappears. The set is defensible as sector names but flattering as a valuation anchor.

answers.question: check receivables and inventory against the sales growth
answers.answer: Receivables corroborate the cash-flow worry: at ~118 days latest (worse at ~158 days the prior year), receivables are growing at least in line with the 45% sales growth, so a rising share of reported revenue is uncollected. I was given no inventory figure, so I cannot test the inventory side — its absence is notable given working capital is clearly absorbing the reported profits.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A note showing receivables are contractually milestone-billed and being collected post year-end (plus an ageing schedule with no ballooning >180-day bucket) would substantially upgrade the long-term view; conversely, evidence that the fresh-issue proceeds primarily fund working capital rather than capacity, or adverse detail in the promoter criminal-proceedings sections [litigation, page 420], would push it lower.
